issues.legal_issue: The deletion of former rulers from the statutory definition of a person did not exempt them from agricultural income tax.
material_facts: The agricultural income tax law imposed tax on the total agricultural income of every person and expressly exempted government and local-authority income, but not the income of former rulers.
The original definition of a person expressly included a ruler of an Indian State; a later adaptation deleted that reference after the former Indian States had ceased to exist.
The former ruler was assessed on agricultural income and relied on the deletion to claim that he was not a person liable to tax.
issues.conclusion: The deletion did not show an intention to exclude former rulers from tax liability, and the absence of an express exemption meant the former ruler remained liable to tax.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 2(i) and 3 of the Orissa Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1947, tax was imposed on the agricultural income of every person, subject to the stated exemptions. The deletion of the reference to rulers by the Adaptation of Laws Order, 1950, reflected political changes and did not create an exemption. An exemption cannot be inferred merely because the amended definition no longer expressly refers to former rulers.

rule.if: agricultural_income_tax_assessment and income_tax_imposed_on_every_person and subject_is_former_ruler and ruler_reference_deleted_after_political_change and no_express_exemption

predicates.agricultural_income_tax_assessment: The proceeding concerns an assessment of tax on agricultural income.
predicates.income_tax_imposed_on_every_person: The applicable tax rule imposes liability on every person receiving the income in question, subject to specified exemptions.
predicates.subject_is_former_ruler: The person assessed formerly held the status of a ruler.
predicates.ruler_reference_deleted_after_political_: A later amendment removed an express reference to rulers after the political status of the former states had changed.
predicates.no_express_exemption: The applicable law contains no express exemption for the assessed person or class.

issues.definition: When an agricultural-income tax assessment concerns a former ruler, the tax applies to every person, the ruler reference was deleted after political change, and no express exemption exists, the former ruler remains taxable.

issues.legal_issue: A guarantee of personal privileges to a former ruler does not exempt the ruler's private property from taxation.
material_facts: The merger agreement guaranteed the former ruler ownership and enjoyment of private property and separately guaranteed personal privileges, rights, dignities, and titles.
The former ruler claimed that his pre-merger immunity from taxation was protected by those guarantees.
The tax assessment was imposed on agricultural income from his private property.
issues.conclusion: The guaranteed privileges were personal privileges of the former ruler and did not extend to his private property; the guarantees did not exempt that property from tax.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 4 and 5 of the merger agreement concerned personal privileges and rights of the ruler, not immunity of private property from taxation. The Court followed Visweshwar Rao v. The State of Madhya Pradesh, [1952] S.C.R. 1020, which distinguished a ruler's personal rights from personal property. Article 362 did not alter the scope of the guarantees so as to create a property-tax exemption.

predicates.tax_assessment_dispute: The proceeding concerns a tax assessment challenged by the person assessed.
predicates.merger_agreement_guarantees_personal_pri: An agreement made on a state's merger guarantees personal rights or privileges to its former ruler.
predicates.tax_targets_private_property: The tax is imposed on income derived from the former ruler's private property.

issues.definition: When a tax assessment targets private property and a merger agreement guarantees personal privileges, the guarantee does not exempt the private property from tax.

issues.legal_issue: A claim seeking to enforce a former ruler's agreement-based immunity from taxation is not justiciable when it challenges the exercise of legislative authority by relying on that agreement.
material_facts: The former ruler invoked the merger agreement to resist the application of the agricultural income tax law to his private-property income.
He sought relief in court on the basis that the tax law and its enforcement were contrary to the agreement.
The claim asked the court to give effect to the agreement's guarantees against the taxing action.
issues.conclusion: The claim based on the merger agreement was not justiciable.
issues.legal_principle: Article 362 directs legislatures and executive authorities to have due regard to guarantees in relevant agreements but does not create an enforceable legal obligation at the former ruler's instance. Article 363 provides that legislative authority cannot be questioned in court by relying on such an agreement. The Court held that the claim, though framed as resistance to taxation, sought to enforce the merger agreement.

predicates.agreement_based_tax_challenge: The person assessed challenges a tax action by relying on an agreement made with a former ruler.
predicates.claim_seeks_enforcement_of_ruler_agreeme: The relief sought would require a court to enforce a guarantee in the agreement.
predicates.challenge_contests_exercise_of_legislati: The claim asks a court to question the exercise of legislative authority on the basis of the agreement.

issues.definition: When a tax challenge seeks enforcement of a former ruler's agreement and contests legislative authority on that basis, the agreement-based claim is not justiciable.

issues.legal_issue: Factual grounds that were not raised before the High Court cannot be considered for the first time in an appeal from a tax assessment decision.
material_facts: The former ruler argued on appeal that income from two villages transferred to a family member should not be included in his assessment, although that claim had not been raised in the High Court.

He also argued that the assessment should be limited to villages listed in an inventory, although that claim had not been raised in the High Court and no evidence or finding on it was before the Supreme Court.
The Supreme Court was hearing appeals from the High Court's decisions on the assessments.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected both grounds because they had not been raised in the High Court and could not be examined for the first time in those appeals.
issues.legal_principle: An appellate court will not enter into a factual inquiry on a claim that was not raised before the High Court, particularly where the opposing party had no opportunity to meet it and the High Court made no finding on it.

predicates.appeal_from_tax_assessment_decision: The proceeding is an appeal from a decision concerning a tax assessment.
predicates.factual_ground_not_raised_before_high_co: The appellant did not raise the factual ground in the High Court.
predicates.no_high_court_finding_on_ground: The High Court made no finding on the factual ground.

issues.definition: In an appeal from a tax assessment decision, a factual ground not raised before the High Court and not decided there is not considered on appeal.
